habit_line: Focus habit: Look back - Ask what was learnt and what they would change, after the work is done. Say: “What did you learn? What would you do differently next time?” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: Welcome, inquirers! Today we play games and then ask the big question: is this game fair? Our feelings are not enough. We will count outcomes with fractions, and then make the computer play a game a thousand times to test our maths.
do: Focus habit: Look back - Ask what was learnt and what they would change, after the work is done. Say: “What did you learn? What would you do differently next time?” Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

say: Here is a line from 0 to 1. 0 means impossible, 1 means certain, 1/2 means an even chance.
For each card, decide where it goes on the line and give its fraction. Take as long as you need, and point to the line first. There is no timer.
In the Dice Race, player A wins on six totals: 2, 3, 4, 10, 11, 12. Player B wins on only five: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. Who do you think will win more often? Write A, B or “same”, and a reason.
stuck: Keep a tally: one column for A, one for B. Write the total each time.
Surprised by your results? Write down which totals came up most.
Finished early: in how many ways can two dice make a total of 7? Of 2? Use a red die and a blue die so 1 + 6 and 6 + 1 are different.

say: “Roll one dice. More than 4 means 5 or 6: that is 2 ways out of 6 equally likely outcomes. So the probability is 2/6, which is 1/3.”

“Two dice. The red die has 6 outcomes and for each one the blue die has 6, so 6 × 6 = 36, just like last lesson’s nested loop. A total of 7 happens 6 times: 1 + 6, 2 + 5, 3 + 4, 4 + 3, 5 + 2, 6 + 1. So P(7) = 6/36 = 1/6. A total of 2 happens once: 1/36.”

“In 1000 games I expect B to win about 2/3 × 1000, which is 666 2/3. A count cannot be 666 2/3, and every run is random, so the program will say something close, like 670 or 649, but almost never exactly 667.”

do: Ask: “What are the equally likely outcomes here? How many are there?”
Ask: “What fraction do you expect? So about how many out of 1000?”
Ask: “Your program said 158, not 167. Is it broken? How could you check?” (run it again; run 10 000 games and look at the fraction)
stuck: Hint 1: “List every outcome. Are they all equally likely?”
Hint 2: “For two dice, draw the 6 by 6 table.”
Hint 3: “Expected number = probability × number of tries.”

say: “Mei flipped a coin 10 times and got 7 heads. She says the coin is unfair. Do you agree?”
“How many flips would you need before you believed her? How could a program help?”
ask: “Mei flipped a coin 10 times and got 7 heads. She says the coin is unfair. Do you agree?”

Not yet: 10 flips is far too few. With a fair coin, 7 or more heads in 10 flips happens 176 times in 1024, about 1 time in 6. To test it, flip many more times (or simulate 1000 flips of a fair coin to see how much the counts wobble). If 1000 real flips gave 700 heads, that would be strong evidence: a fair coin almost never does that.

say: “Today you measured chance with fractions, found the hidden unfairness in a game, and let the computer play a thousand games to test your maths. Close, not exact: that is how random things behave.”

p6l6-title.note: Objective: Write a probability as a fraction (ways it can happen out of equally likely outcomes), list all 36 outcomes for two dice, decide whether a game is fair, change a game to make it fair, and run a game 1000 times in code, explaining why the result is close to what we expect but not exact. Materials: Laptop or desktop with Scratch 3 (scratch.mit.edu), two dice per pair (or the tutor’s dice program, in the starter file L6_Chance_Lab.sb3), a coin, coloured counters and a paper bag, mini whiteboards, tally sheet. Online: Children roll real dice at home; anyone without dice builds the dice program live in the shared Scratch window (pick random 1 to 6, twice) and uses that, or opens the starter file L6_Chance_Lab.sb3 (File, Load from your computer; no account needed): press the d key to roll two dice and see the total, and click the green flag to run the coin program of Q2. This lesson is enrichment: probability is new to most children, so keep it playful. Block colours on our slides are simplified; in Scratch, find blocks by the category name on the left, not by colour. Pairs play the Explore game in breakout rooms and type their tallies into the chat so the group total can be added up. Time plan (the exact minutes of this lesson, with a standing flex buffer): opening 0 to 2, sneak-peek puzzles 2 to 6.5, warm-up 6.5 to 12.5, explore 12.5 to 27 (play the Dice Race, then pool the results), mini-lesson 27 to 37.5 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 37.5 to 42.5, worksheet 42.5 to 74 with short teaching before each page and a check-together slide after it, flex 74 to 76.5 (unscripted: use it for Think harder or catch-up; it is lost first), talk time 76.5 to 82.5, exit slip 82.5 to 86, looking back 86 to 88, close and stamp 88 to 90. Before the lesson: have the Explore game program ready to share (Scratch, below on the teach-code slide) and a dice program for children without dice. SPINE: Today's tool is Act it out. Model or simulate the situation (objects, fold, cut, dice) and record the outcomes. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook. HABIT: Focus habit: Look back. Ask what was learnt and what they would change, after the work is done. Say: "What did you learn? What would you do differently next time?" Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.

p6l6-check.note: Minutes 2 to 6.5. These are ideas we have not learnt yet: say so, and say that guessing and "I do not know" are welcome and nobody is marked. Read the two puzzles aloud. Puzzle 1 is an access puzzle: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone can get a first win. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle on today's idea. ONE check moment only: after both puzzles, everyone says the answers together on three (nothing is held up to the camera). Never private chat. Never compare answers across children, never read wrong answers aloud. Then click to reveal the answers one after the other and move on with no reaction round: say each answer in 15 words or fewer, then say: "Both of these are what we learn today." Answers: Puzzle 1: Blue, because there are more blue counters (5 out of 8) than red (3 out of 8). Drawing the counters is enough. Puzzle 2: Fair. The four outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT. Match: HH and TT (2 out of 4). Different: HT and TH (2 out of 4). A guess is welcome; the list decides. Invite the WHOLE group, never one child: say "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Nobody is singled out. Any child can choose it and any child can go back. Never announce who is on which page and never say advanced or top group. Do not record this as a mark. Do not split a pair unless both children agree.

p6l6-warm1.note: Minutes 6.5 to 10. Where on the line? Pairs place four events on a 0 to 1 probability line and give each one’s fraction: roll a 7, flip heads, pick a vowel from SINGAPORE, roll 1 to 6. Pairs agree on a spot and a fraction for each card (no timer), then click to drop the marker (markers appear A to D; four events only, so the warm-up fits). Answers: A 0 (impossible). B 1/2. C 4/9 (I, A, O, E are 4 of the 9 letters). D 1 (certain). Ask: "Is C more or less than an even chance?" (4/9 is a little less than 1/2, because 4.5/9 would be 1/2.) "Can a probability be 6/5?" (No: never more than 1, never less than 0.) Key words for today: equally likely outcomes, fair, expect.

p6l6-warm2.note: Minutes 10 to 12.5. Fraction warm-up: we use all of these today. Whiteboards, then click. Three questions only. Answers: 1) 1/6 2) 100 3) 4/9 (16/36 is more than 15/36). For 3, compare using a common denominator of 36.

p6l6-explore1.note: Minutes 12.5 to 27 (this slide 12.5 to 17). The Dice Race: roll two dice and add. Player A wins on 2, 3, 4, 10, 11 or 12; player B wins on 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9. Pairs predict, play 20 rounds, tally the wins, then add up the whole group’s results. Predict first: In the Dice Race, player A wins on six totals: 2, 3, 4, 10, 11, 12. Player B wins on only five: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9. Who do you think will win more often? Write A, B or “same”, and a reason. Hints: Keep a tally: one column for A, one for B. Write the total each time. Surprised by your results? Write down which totals came up most. If a pair wants more: in how many ways can two dice make a total of 7? Of 2? Use a red die and a blue die so 1 + 6 and 6 + 1 are different. Online: Children roll real dice at home; anyone without dice builds the dice program live in the shared Scratch window (pick random 1 to 6, twice) and uses that, or opens the starter file L6_Chance_Lab.sb3 (File, Load from your computer; no account needed): press the d key to roll two dice and see the total, and click the green flag to run the coin program of Q2. This lesson is enrichment: probability is new to most children, so keep it playful. Block colours on our slides are simplified; in Scratch, find blocks by the category name on the left, not by colour. Pairs play the Explore game in breakout rooms and type their tallies into the chat so the group total can be added up. While pairs play, add up the class tallies on a shared slide or in the chat. Expect B to win about 2 rounds in every 3, but a single pair's 20 rounds can easily come out level or even favour A: that is why we pool the results. Go further what-if (not a slide: paste it in the chat for any pair that finishes early, and take it up only if a pair wants to share): What if A wins on totals 2 to 6 and B wins on totals 7 to 12? Predict who wins more often. Play 10 rounds, then explain using the 36 outcomes. Answer: B is more likely: totals 7 to 12 can be made in 21 of the 36 ways, totals 2 to 6 in only 15 (so 21/36 = 7/12 against 15/36 = 5/12). The game is not fair.

p6l6-explore2.note: Minutes 17 to 27. Show the pooled tallies. Answers: 1) Usually B. The group total is closer to B winning about 2 rounds in every 3. 2) The totals are not equally likely: 7 can be made in 6 ways, 2 in only 1 way. B’s totals can be made in 24 of the 36 ways. Do not reveal the 36-outcome table yet: it comes in the teaching. Two questions only. Ask: "If a pair got A 11, B 9, does that prove A is luckier?" (No: 20 games is a small sample.)

p6l6-teach1.note: Minutes 27 to 28.5. Teach. Think-aloud: “Roll one dice. More than 4 means 5 or 6: that is 2 ways out of 6 equally likely outcomes. So the probability is 2/6, which is 1/3.” Stress EQUALLY LIKELY: "Each face of a fair dice has the same chance. That is why we can just count." Ask: "Is P(win the lottery) = 1/2 because you either win or you don't?" (No: the two outcomes are not equally likely.)

p6l6-we1.note: Minutes 28.5 to 30. Click through. Ask before step 2: "What fraction is yellow?" Before step 3: "If we spin 600 times, how many yellows should we expect?" Then: "Will it be exactly 200?" Collect a few guesses; we test this with code in a moment. P(blue) = 3/6 = 1/2, P(red) = 1/6: the three add up to 1.

p6l6-try1.note: Minutes 30 to 31. Whiteboards. a) 3 out of 10. b) not blue = red or green = 5 out of 10 = 1/2 (or 1 − 5/10). c) 2, 3 and 5 are prime (1 is not prime): 3/6 = 1/2.

p6l6-teachtwo.note: Minutes 31 to 33. Teach. Use a red die and a blue die so that 1 + 6 and 6 + 1 are clearly different outcomes. Think-aloud: “Two dice. The red die has 6 outcomes and for each one the blue die has 6, so 6 × 6 = 36, just like last lesson’s nested loop. A total of 7 happens 6 times: 1 + 6, 2 + 5, 3 + 4, 4 + 3, 5 + 2, 6 + 1. So P(7) = 6/36 = 1/6. A total of 2 happens once: 1/36.” Then link to the Explore: "A has more TOTALS, but B has more OUTCOMES." Common wrong idea: "there are 11 totals, so each is 1/11". Totals are not equally likely; the 36 outcomes are.

p6l6-try2.note: Minutes 33 to 34. Children look at the table. a) 5 + 6 and 6 + 5. b) 1 + 3, 2 + 2, 3 + 1. c) 10, 11 or 12: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 ways. Ask: "Which total is most likely? Least likely?" (7; 2 and 12).

p6l6-teachcode.note:
Minutes 34 to 36.5. Teach the code and, in the bottom panel, why the runs are close but not exact (the old separate slide is folded in: five runs of 600 rolls counting 6s gave 102, 101, 85, 103 and 97 against an expected 100; about 9 runs in 10 land between 85 and 115; more rolls make the FRACTION of 6s closer to 1/6). Share your screen and run it 2 or 3 times. Point out "pick random 1 to 6" is one dice roll; adding two of them is two dice (NOT "pick random 2 to 12", which would make every total equally likely: a good question to ask!). Think-aloud: “In 1000 games I expect B to win about 2/3 × 1000, which is 666 2/3. A count cannot be 666 2/3, and every run is random, so the program will say something close, like 670 or 649, but almost never exactly 667.” The three runs on the slide are real results from 1000-game runs; yours will differ. This is our main program today. Python version:
import random
a_wins = 0
b_wins = 0
for game in range(1000):
 d1 = random.randint(1, 6)
 d2 = random.randint(1, 6)
 if 5 <= d1 + d2 <= 9:
 b_wins = b_wins + 1
 else:
 a_wins = a_wins + 1
print(a_wins, b_wins)

p6l6-key.note: Minutes 36.5 to 37.5. Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Treating outcomes as equally likely when they are not (two coins: “two heads, two tails, one of each” as thirds; dice totals 2 to 12 as elevenths). (2) Thinking a random result should come out exactly as expected, or that a coin “is due” a head after several tails. (3) Not simplifying, or writing the number of ways instead of the fraction (6 instead of 6/36 = 1/6).

p6l6-break.note: Minutes 37.5 to 42.5. 5 minutes. Roll about 6 times. Afterwards ask: "Did we do each move twice? Should we have?" (Not necessarily: 6 rolls is a tiny sample.) Online: children stay in view of the camera.

p6l6-teachbag.note: Minutes 42.5 to 44.5. Teach before worksheet page 1 (Q3 changes a bag of 4 red and 6 blue: do not do those numbers here). Use real counters in a bag if you can. Think-aloud: "For P(red) = 1/4, the red counters are 1 part out of 4 parts. 2 red is one part, so 4 parts is 8 counters. I have 6, so I add 2 blue." Check by writing the new fraction and simplifying. Counters with a thick outline are the new ones.

p6l6-ws1.note: Minutes 44.5 to 54.5. Walk around. Ask "What are the equally likely outcomes? How many?" Children who finish Q2 build the coin program and compare their 3 runs with their partner's.

p6l6-ws1ans.note: Minutes 54.5 to 57.5. All the answers are shown at once. Children mark in a different colour; ask ONE volunteer to explain only Q1 (random results wobble), about 35 seconds a question. Q1d: with a fair 3/8 spinner, about 19 runs in 20 land between 345 and 405 reds, and about 1 run in 5 gives 362 or fewer. Q2b: exactly 500 heads happens only about 1 run in 40. Q3c: 4 red must be 1/5 of the total, so the total is 20: add 10 blue. Full key: (a) 3/8 (b) 6/8 = 3/4 (c) about 375 (3/8 × 1000) (d) No. Each spin is random, so the count wobbles around 375; 362 is close. About 19 runs in 20 land between 345 and 405. | (a) about 500 (1/2 × 1000) (b) No. The flips are random, so each run gives a slightly different count near 500. Exactly 500 happens only about 1 run in 40. (c) about 200 (1/5 × 1000) | (a) 4/10 = 2/5 (b) 2 red (6 red, 6 blue: 6/12 = 1/2) (the “add blue to make 1/5” part is now in Think harder 4)

p6l6-teachfair.note: Minutes 57.5 to 60.5. Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4, the Difference Game: do not do it here; the bottom panel is the Q5 code plan, folded in). For the code: each coin needs its own random number (one pick random for both coins would make them always the same); if time, run it: answers near 500 (e.g. 489, 512) confirm the game is fair. Ask first: "Fair or not? Thumbs up or down." Many say Ali wins only 1/3 (two heads, two tails versus one of each). Use two different coins (a 10¢ and a 20¢) so HT and TH are clearly different. Then: "How could we change an unfair game to make it fair?" (change which outcomes win, or give different points).

p6l6-ws2.note: Minutes 60.5 to 71.5. Children work alone. Show this preview, do not read it aloud. Note who needs a short catch-up next lesson. Children who finish change the Explore program (or the Python corner) to play the Difference Game 1000 times and check their answer to Q4.

p6l6-ws2ans.note: Minutes 71.5 to 74. All the answers are shown at once. Children mark in a different colour; ask ONE volunteer to explain only Q4 (why is the Difference Game unfair?). Q4: other fair rules: Ali on 1 and 2 (10 + 8 = 18); or Ali on 0, 1 and 5 (6 + 10 + 2 = 18). Ask: "Each player had 3 differences. Why was it still unfair?" Q5: about 19 runs in 20 land between 145 and 190 doubles. Full key: (a) Differences: 0 appears 6 times, 1: 10, 2: 8, 3: 6, 4: 4, 5: 2 (36 in all). (b) Ali 24/36 = 2/3, Ben 12/36 = 1/3 (c) Not fair: Ali is twice as likely to win, even though each has 3 differences. (Making it fair is now in Think harder 4.) | Gaps: 6, 6, a = b. (a) About 167: P(double) = 6/36 = 1/6, and 1/6 × 1000 = 166 2/3. (b) A count must be a whole number, and each run is random, so it lands near 167 (about 19 runs in 20 between 145 and 190), not exactly on it.

p6l6-stretch.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Extra questions for any pair that wants them (these are not on the Think harder page). Answers: 1) 2/11 2) About 400 (2 of the 6 results are bigger than 4, and 1/3 × 1200 = 400). 391 is close, so nothing is wrong: a random simulation is never exactly the expected number. 3) 11/36 (6 with the red die, 6 with the blue die, minus the 6 + 6 counted twice: 6 + 6 − 1 = 11)

p6l6-challenge.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. These are also on the Go further page. Answers: 1) Not fair. Mei wins 15/36 = 5/12; Ali wins 21/36 = 7/12 (15 bigger + 6 the same). Fair version: the same number means roll again. 2) Not fair. There are 3 × 4 = 12 outcomes; the answer is odd only when both are odd: 2 × 2 = 4 ways. P(Odd) = 4/12 = 1/3, P(Even) = 8/12 = 2/3.

p6l6-chdiag.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Show after pairs have tried, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: How many equally likely outcomes are there? Which squares does Mei win? What has to be true for a product to be odd?

p6l6-chwalk.note: Optional, if you finish early (no clock time): show it only while some children are working, never as a group slide at a fixed minute. Use after pairs have tried. Q1: with "roll again on the same number", each player wins 15 of the 30 remaining outcomes: fair. Q2: test it in code: set a to pick random 1 to 3, set b to pick random 1 to 4, check whether a × b is odd (a × b mod 2 = 1); 1000 games give about 333 odd. Ask: "How could you change the spinners to make the game fair?"

p6l6-talk.note: Minutes 76.5 to 82.5. Both questions are kept in this lesson (it has the time). Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Follow-up: “How many flips would you need before you believed her? How could a program help?” Answer: Not yet: 10 flips is far too few. With a fair coin, 7 or more heads in 10 flips happens 176 times in 1024, about 1 time in 6. To test it, flip many more times (or simulate 1000 flips of a fair coin to see how much the counts wobble). If 1000 real flips gave 700 heads, that would be strong evidence: a fair coin almost never does that. Close: “Today you measured chance with fractions, found the hidden unfairness in a game, and let the computer play a thousand games to test your maths. Close, not exact: that is how random things behave.”

p6l6-exit.note: Minutes 82.5 to 86. Answer: 5/36 (2+6, 3+5, 4+4, 5+3, 6+2); about 50 (5/36 × 360 = 50). Extension: Change the Dice Race so that it is fair, using totals only (a total of 7 may mean “roll again”). Test your rules in code with 1000 games. How close to 500 : 500 do you get?

p6l6-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 86 to 88. Start the timer (75 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. After the look-back, minutes 88 to 90 are flex time (the buffer): finish stamps, then goodbye. Do not start anything new. HABIT: Focus habit: Look back. Ask what was learnt and what they would change, after the work is done. Say: "What did you learn? What would you do differently next time?" Do not give the answer first: ask the prompt, wait, and give a hint only if the child is stuck.
